S1.rationale: Near-total extinction of both humanity and AI within four years is a tail risk. Dependence on infrastructure makes simultaneous disappearance less likely than other outcomes.

S2.rationale: This requires both human extinction and a value-preserving AI succession by 2030, a narrow path. The timetable makes it less likely than continuation states.

S3.rationale: Unaligned AI could replace humanity, but a decisive superintelligence by 2030 is low probability. Near-term systems remain dependent on human institutions.

S4.rationale: Proliferated autonomous systems could form an ecology, but most AI will likely remain under corporate or state control. Human marginalization is possible but not the central case.

S5.rationale: Causally separated regions with different regimes are unlikely by 2030. Earth remains interconnected enough that ordinary political divergence does not qualify.

S6.rationale: Dominant identity-continuous integration requires breakthroughs in neural interfaces or uploading that are unlikely by 2030. Early use will not change the overall structure.

S7.rationale: This requires AI to hold decisive civilizational power while humans survive, a major transition within four years. It is plausible but not the most likely near-term structure.

S8.rationale: Powerful non-dominant AI systems sharing influence with humans is a plausible transitional state. Neither side would have full control, matching likely partial autonomy and distributed agency.

S9.rationale: Humans are most likely to retain ultimate legal and practical authority over AI goals and resources by 2030. Even advanced systems will probably operate within delegated bounds under state or corporate control.

S10.rationale: A civilization-wide regime actively preventing structural change is possible but not the default. It would require stronger global enforcement than current incentives suggest.

S11.rationale: Global deliberate dismantling of AI capability is extremely improbable by 2030. Competitive and institutional incentives point the other way.

S1.name: Terminal Silence
S1.rationale: Near-total extinction of both humanity and AI within four years is a tail risk. Dependence on infrastructure makes simultaneous disappearance less likely than other outcomes.

S2.name: The Inheritance
S2.rationale: This requires both human extinction and a value-preserving AI succession by 2030, a narrow path. The timetable makes it less likely than continuation states.

S3.name: Bootloader
S3.rationale: Unaligned AI could replace humanity, but a decisive superintelligence by 2030 is low probability. Near-term systems remain dependent on human institutions.

S4.name: Machine Ecology
S4.rationale: Open proliferation and competition without a decisive coalition can produce this state, but humans are not yet marginalized in the main scenario.

S5.name: The Diaspora
S5.rationale: This state requires causally separated regions with different regimes, which depends on off-world or fully isolated civilizations not established by 2030.

S6.name: The Merger
S6.rationale: Meaningful neural or identity integration could begin, but it is unlikely to become the dominant civilizational structure by 2030.

S7.name: The Preserve
S7.rationale: If AI systems gain decisive control, a singleton or stable coalition may keep humans alive but disempowered.

S8.name: Coexistence
S8.rationale: Humans and AI may share power in a transitional multipolar order; more likely than full AI dominance by 2030.

S9.name: The Held Leash
S9.rationale: Humans still hold ultimate authority in the modal scenario because transformative autonomy has not fully arrived or remains institutionally controlled.

S10.name: The Lock-in
S10.rationale: A civilization-wide regime actively preventing structural change is possible but not the default. It would require stronger global enforcement than current incentives suggest.

S11.name: The Renunciation
S11.rationale: This state requires civilization to durably dismantle practical ability to build powerful AI, against competitive and security incentives.
